1.heading:
Design Systems:
The Solution to Product Collaboration
1.subtitle: As a product person, I love using this diagram to share the product design and development process—teams often face this dilemma.

content.paragraph1: As a product person, I love using this diagram to share the product design and development process—teams often face this dilemma: When designers craft excellent UI/UX, entering the development phase often leads to communication loops with engineers. Due to product launch pressures, the final result ends up being a compromised version.
content.paragraph2: This dilemma persists whether it was 10 years ago or today. Actually, this isn't a problem with designers or engineers—it's a difference in goals and perspectives. As a product designer, I've experienced this countless times. During my 6 years working in Singapore, I gradually explored design systems and discovered they're an effective way to solve this pain point. Design systems ensure consistency between designers and engineers through standardized specifications, significantly reducing communication costs and improving development efficiency.
content.paragraph3: Design systems may sound complex, but they're actually not. Simply put, it's like building with blocks—invest time upfront to create the blocks, then flexibly assemble products later. For product teams, this not only reduces communication and labor costs but also allows teams to focus on innovation and product optimization rather than getting bogged down in minor communication details.

2.heading: Bridging the Gap Between Design and Development
2.subtitle: Communication between designers and engineers sometimes feels like two parallel worlds.

content.paragraph1: Two years ago, I shared design system insights at IxDA. In product design and development pain points, the core issue often stems from product designers and engineers approaching design and development from different perspectives, leading to various frictions and disagreements. My UI and feature designs were often rejected by engineers saying 'this can't be done' or 'that's not practical.' To understand the essence of product development, I started learning front-end development and gradually understood the perspective gap between designers and engineers.
content.paragraph2: Designers' pain point is that their designs often lose their original appearance after development, with some features being compromised or modified. Engineers' frustration is that design specs lack consistency—buttons and text details vary slightly across different pages, increasing maintenance difficulty. Designers and engineers have vastly different backgrounds. Engineers' task is to ensure features are completed on time, while designers pursue visual and experience optimization. This difference makes product specification crucial, especially the convergence and integration of design elements. But relying solely on design specs from designers hardly solves the problem because engineers aren't familiar with visual layout configurations and aesthetic details—this is where the UX Engineer role comes from.
content.paragraph3: Therefore, the core value of design systems isn't just visual specifications, but a component library with code and demos that increases engineers' willingness to use design systems, reduces their investment in visual details, and lets engineers focus more on product feature development.

3.heading: The Art of Design Decluttering
3.subtitle: Design systems are essentially a process of 'integration and quantification.'

content.paragraph1: My dad once told me a story about his childhood when his family was very poor—it left a deep impression. He said they could only afford three tubes of watercolor paint, but with just those three colors, he won second place in the school watercolor competition 😂 This story is actually very similar to product design. Sometimes we feel there are too many rules and constraints—won't they limit UI/UX creativity and prevent us from creating features and interfaces users love? But think about it differently: rules are like those paint tubes. If you make good use of limited resources, you can still create new possibilities through flexible combinations!
content.paragraph2: As products mature, this 'design decluttering' becomes even more important. We need to start converging similar colors, elements, text, and even numbers—quantifying them. We don't let numbers expand infinitely because each number must have a confirmed purpose. For example, with font sizes: 10 might be the smallest text, 14 is default text, 24 is heading text... We need to clearly assign their purposes. The same goes for colors—they won't be expanded without reason.
content.paragraph3: Why? Because in later product stages, components and features only multiply. Infinite expansion only makes projects more complex, development difficulty skyrockets, and ultimately increases labor costs and time. Instead, it's better to converge early, making complex things simple, efficient, and flexible, allowing products to maintain stable output throughout their evolution.

4.heading:
Implementing Design Systems:
A Mountain Worth Climbing
4.subtitle: Implementing a design system in a product team is challenging—like climbing a mountain, but the view from the top is absolutely worth it.

content.paragraph1: I recently listened to @vktechread share about The Hard Thing About Hard Things, and it really resonated with me. To simplify work and improve efficiency, we must first go through the most difficult challenges—like implementing a design system in a product team. Although it feels like climbing a mountain at first, requiring extensive communication, integration, and research, it's precisely these processes that bring the greatest value.
content.paragraph2: As product scale grows, technical debt and system complexity make development time longer and costs higher. When I worked at enterprises, I often saw large development teams spending 60-70% of their resources maintaining old architectures rather than innovating or optimizing products.
content.paragraph3: This is exactly where design systems prove their worth. After implementation, product development becomes more like assembling blocks, eliminating the tedious 'clay molding' process and simplifying communication and workflows. Teams can then focus on product innovation rather than getting caught up in minor details. In business competition, speed matters. Shortening development time and quickly entering the market to test and iterate not only improves efficiency and reduces costs but is also key to winning for companies and products.

5.heading: Work Hard & Smart
5.subtitle: Work hard? Work smart? Combining both seems even better!

content.paragraph1: I really love this animation about work from overseas. Just like when we first enter the workforce, most of us approach every task with full dedication, hoping to do our best. As experience accumulates and we enter mid-career, we start finding clever ways to simplify processes and improve efficiency. In the mature stage of our careers, we gradually realize there's no such thing as 'easy' work, but through accumulated experience, we can combine hard work with smart work to achieve excellent results with half the effort.
content.paragraph2: The design system workflow is similar. Building a design system is often challenging at first, but once completed and integrated into the product development process, it becomes like the Work Hard & Smart animation in this video—the work mode becomes smooth and efficient, simplifying work while significantly improving product quality and consistency.
content.paragraph3: So, instead of choosing between working hard or working smart, consider how to combine both to make work more efficient while also gaining a sense of achievement.

6.heading:
Design Token:
The Shared Language of Design and Development
6.subtitle: Design Tokens can become a shared configuration file between design and development.

content.paragraph1: During the online briefing for the design system course, I discovered many questions I hadn't thought of before. Many people asked how to convert Figma designs into UI component libraries (Storybook) code and sync them, and whether designers need to know coding to maintain frontend component libraries.
content.paragraph2: In my view, designers don't necessarily need to write code or use tools that generate code directly from Figma, as the output code may not be complete. However, in product teams, designers and engineers can plan Design Tokens together. Design Tokens are like a shared configuration file between design and development, and Figma's new Variables feature is designed to set up and manage these tokens. This way, from design to development, you can painlessly connect parameters to the code-side Variables through Figma Variables export or sync, achieving component style synchronization.
content.paragraph3: I encourage designers to learn some front-end development knowledge—it helps understand product development logic better. Design can be output quickly, but understanding how to actually execute within limited resources and time matters. Knowing some programming thinking makes collaboration between design and development smoother! In this design system course, Design Token is the longest module XD

7.heading:
Design Token Naming:
The Art of Three-Layer Structure
7.subtitle: Design Token naming is abstract—design and engineering teams can collaborate to establish clear, consistent naming conventions.

content.paragraph1: Continuing the Design Token discussion, Design Token planning requires collaboration between designers and engineers to ensure naming conventions and structural consistency. Using Google Material Design as an example, Design Tokens are divided into three layers: First is the design system prefix—for example, 'ABC Design System' can use 'abcd' as a prefix, where 'd' stands for Design System; Second is the Token type, including Reference (base values like colors, font sizes), System (semantic properties like primary or secondary), and Component (component-level properties like button background color); Third is the role and purpose, explaining which properties the Token is used for, such as color, border-radius, or spacing.
content.paragraph2: Reference and Component Token naming is intuitive, while System Tokens require more consensus due to their abstract nature. Regardless of the planning approach, the order of each layer structure must be consistent to make naming conventions more intuitive and improve search efficiency.
content.paragraph3: Because of course planning, I also developed a small Design Token naming tool that uses multiple-choice questions to better understand the naming and logic sequence.

8.heading:
Token Inheritance:
The Chef's Special Wisdom
8.subtitle: Design Token inheritance systems can improve flexibility and scalability while reducing maintenance costs.

content.paragraph1: A student asked about the inheritance relationship between different levels of Design tokens and what the difference would be without inheritance. Let's start with Ref tokens—naming at this layer is very intuitive, like red is red, blue is blue. But if you use Ref tokens directly in components or text, when you need to adjust colors or styles in the future, you'll have to find and modify every place using that token. This is exactly why we need the second semantic token layer—to provide flexibility and error tolerance.
content.paragraph2: Here's an example: In a restaurant menu, if the dish name is 'Steak,' the ingredient can only be beef. If beef runs out one day and needs to be changed to pork, the restaurant must change the dish name to 'Pork Chop.' But if the dish name was 'Chef's Special' from the start, whether it's changed to pork, chicken, or other ingredients in the future, it can be easily swapped without changing the menu name each time. This is the purpose of semantic Token naming with inheritance—improving flexibility and reducing modification costs.
content.paragraph3: In practice, Design tokens are usually created in different files. Through a semantic inheritance system, engineers can make unified adjustments at the Sys Token layer without modifying style code in every component file, improving maintenance efficiency. However, not all projects need a 3-layer inheritance structure. For small to medium projects, Ref to Sys two layers are sufficient. The key is communicating with the engineering team to ensure methods are synchronized ✨

9.heading:
Token Semantics:
Unified Naming System
9.subtitle: Systematizing Design Token semantics reduces confusion when referencing.

content.paragraph1: Recently, while reviewing students' Design Token design assignments in the course, I found a common challenge is Design Token state naming, especially in the system semantic part. Since everyone may understand and describe semantics differently, it causes confusion when referencing. To solve this problem, I spent some time organizing commonly used Token state adjectives, such as color brightness/darkness, depth/shallowness, solid to transparent, size, weight, etc.
content.paragraph2: I highly recommend product teams plan similar diagrams and include them in shared project documentation. This way, team members have a unified naming system to reference when designing Design Tokens, reducing confusion when referencing.
content.paragraph3: Additionally, on the engineering side, variable naming has always been a pain point. By systematizing semantics, naming inconsistencies can be greatly reduced, improving overall collaboration efficiency :)

10.heading:
Cross-Team Design Systems:
The Value of Storybook
10.subtitle: What product teams need is a design system that can be used 'across teams.'

content.paragraph1: I've had an experience where even when the design team had a complete design system planned, it ended up being shelved. The main reason is that engineers prioritize product and feature development—unless time is very generous, they rarely read design specifications carefully. Also, engineers who understand visual styles are relatively rare. Therefore, product teams need a system that supports both design and engineering. What is a 'cross-team design system'? In 2016, a startup team from Sri Lanka developed a tool for building design systems and component libraries—Storybook.
content.paragraph2: Fortunately, in 2017, when discussing how to solve collaboration and communication issues between design and technology with the engineering team, the engineers proposed this design system tool that could solve design-engineering communication challenges—Storybook. Since then, I began researching and learning how to build product design systems with Storybook. Storybook's greatest advantage is providing documentation and component management for both designers and engineers: engineers can directly copy component code into projects; designers can view specifications and documentation, ultimately becoming the product team's product Wikipedia.
content.paragraph3: A design system that enables cross-team collaboration and is actively used in products won't become a static design guide left in the corner of the project.

11.heading:
Color Planning:
Less Is More
11.subtitle: When planning colors in design systems, first clarify the purpose of each color before configuration—avoid adding unnecessary color levels.

content.paragraph1: When planning colors for design systems, you must first clarify the actual purpose of each color before making appropriate configurations—avoid adding too many color scales without clear purposes just for color diversity.
content.paragraph2: Compared to Google Material Design, typical projects usually don't need a large number of customizable styles or an overly massive design system. Instead, they plan systems and color elements that match the project scale based on product needs. The core goal of design systems is to improve product team efficiency, so maintaining simplicity and clarity within limited design elements is more important; a simplified design system is easier to truly implement within teams.
content.paragraph3: Of course, we can reference design systems of different scales and their logic, but through moderate streamlining, we avoid unlimited expansion of colors and other elements that make product projects increasingly complex and difficult to maintain. This way, we can maintain the effectiveness and usability of the design system while supporting project development 🤓 Less is more!

12.heading:
Theme Inversion Colors:
Neutral Semantic Naming
12.subtitle: Use neutral semantics/number levels to name inverted color Tokens for light and dark themes in design systems.

content.paragraph1: When designing color Tokens, a common problem is how to reasonably name container and text colors for different light and dark themes. For example, if in the light theme, a black Token is named color-dark, but in the dark theme, this black inverts to white, making the original naming unintuitive.
content.paragraph2: Therefore, it's recommended to use adjective semantics or number levels for naming. For example, in the light theme, black is a 'heavier' tone, and when inverted to white in the dark theme, it still retains this 'heaviness.' In this case, we can use naming methods like Heavy or Level-100, making inverted colors clearer in understanding their position across different themes.

13.heading:
Tool Share:
Color Contrast Checker
13.subtitle: Check if color contrast meets WCAG standards to ensure readability and visual clarity in web design.

content.paragraph1: Today I want to share a simple and easy-to-use tool — Color Contrast Checker (https://coolors.co/contrast-checker). This tool lets you easily test whether the contrast between background and text colors meets standards, ensuring comfortable and clear web reading. Just enter your chosen colors and immediately see their combination effect. Generally, large text in the tool refers to 24px and above, small text is 18px and below, and regular text is approximately between 18px to 24px.
content.paragraph2: Ideal color scoring should reach at least 7 points, and you can intuitively identify compliant color combinations from the tool interface. This tool evaluates color contrast based on WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) standards, specifically setting minimum contrast ratio requirements for different font sizes, enabling more scientific color design that cares for users with special visual needs.
content.paragraph3: Additionally, when designing dark themes, this tool greatly helps you accurately select colors, ensuring every color combination achieves ideal readability.

14.heading:
Icon Design:
Unified Size and Alignment
14.subtitle: When designing or referencing icons, unify sizes and precisely align to grids—to avoid uneven sizes or alignment deviations when exported.

content.paragraph1: When developing design systems, sometimes you encounter issues with inconsistent icon sizes and stroke weights. Because designers sometimes create their own icons and sometimes reference third-party icons, this easily leads to inconsistent sizes and weights, affecting icon-to-text alignment, and even causing blurriness when exporting icon fonts.
content.paragraph2: Therefore, when designing or referencing icons, it's recommended to use a fixed artboard (such as 24x24px), ensuring every pixel aligns to the grid, especially maintaining consistent stroke weight. This way, when engineers implement products, they can better integrate text and icons while maintaining consistent product quality :)

15.heading:
Component Deconstruction:
Extracting Design Elements
15.subtitle: Design systems are a process of deconstruction—extracting core design elements by breaking down components. Each component is composed of diverse design elements.

content.paragraph1: In typical product projects, we usually design components and interfaces first. Although design systems are a quantum design process from micro to macro, we can also work in reverse—starting from interface and component design, then breaking them down into sub-components, and extracting the design elements needed for the project.
content.paragraph2: Using the example in the image, after designing a product information card component, we can further break it down into card, button, title, text, image, and icon components, then extract design elements like colors, font sizes, border-radius, dimensions, spacing, and shadows.
content.paragraph3: After organizing the deconstructed components and elements, they can be integrated into the design system with relevant documentation. Design systems are like building blocks, and these blocks are what we obtain through product deconstruction.

16.heading:
Component Composition:
Flexible Building Block Thinking
16.subtitle: Components in design systems are made up of different elements. When designing components and interfaces, focus on creating flexible components that can be combined into multi-functional assemblies for different scenarios.

content.paragraph1: Continuing the component deconstruction theme, each component is composed of smaller sub-components and elements. We can use this concept to create flexible components through different combinations of elements and components, applying them to various functions and scenarios.
content.paragraph2: For example, a card component can transform into a member card, date card, news card, or description card based on needs. Therefore, when designing components, consider their multiple uses and future assembly possibilities.
content.paragraph3: From an engineer's perspective, achieving multi-functionality through component composition not only shortens repetitive development time but also helps maintain product projects more efficiently.

17.heading:
Clay vs. Blocks:
Two Design Mindsets
17.subtitle: Molding clay is free and fun but hard to replicate; assembling blocks may be more 'boring' but allows for quick, mass reproduction.

content.paragraph1: I recently saw this meme that reminded me of the design system concept: one approach is like freely 'molding clay,' while another is modular like 'building blocks.' The 2009 McDonald's architecture was creative and distinctive but difficult to replicate at scale. In contrast, today's McDonald's appearance may be more 'boring' but can be mass-replicated more efficiently—a choice more aligned with business needs.
content.paragraph2: From a design system perspective, this 'replicable, expandable' model is perfect for products requiring long-term maintenance and expansion. Conversely, marketing websites or campaign projects often prioritize rapid iteration and eye-catching visuals with shorter lifespans, so highly standardized design system processes may not suit them.
content.paragraph3: When businesses expand and product lines diversify, implementing design systems enables teams to maintain and develop more efficiently with smoother collaboration. But neither approach is absolutely better—the key is choosing the most suitable method based on project needs and business stage ✨

18.heading:
AI and Design Systems:
Future Collaboration
18.subtitle: By training AI to learn product design systems and component libraries, it can automatically use these standardized components for assembly, significantly improving automation efficiency.

content.paragraph1: While preparing the design system course, I designed a chapter focusing on using AI to accelerate design system planning and component development. Thinking about this topic reminded me of Figma's future AI design capabilities: having AI help plan products and content based on user needs.
content.paragraph2: Currently, Figma cannot set component library sources, but if this feature opens in the future, AI could reference design systems and related components in product projects, understand their functions and purposes, and automatically design interfaces and features that better match product needs—not just stopping at the wireframe stage.
content.paragraph3: Additionally, AI can help teams develop prototypes faster by learning design system component libraries, even achieving complete products. Therefore, whether conceptually or practically, design systems will play an increasingly important role in the future. Let's look forward to the day when AI fully integrates into product design with more mature applications ✨

19.heading:
Variables and Styles:
An Inseparable Relationship
19.subtitle: In design systems, Design Tokens (Variables) and Styles are inseparable. Design Tokens provide foundational values for Styles, such as colors, fonts, sizes, etc.

content.paragraph1: Recently, a student asked about the difference between Variables and Styles in Figma. Actually, Variables are specific setting values, while Styles are like groups (for example, a button Style contains color, text, size, etc., and these can all reference Design Tokens, which are Variable values).
content.paragraph2: Previously, these values couldn't be centrally managed—you could only set various Styles separately. Now with Figma Variables, you can uniformly store and manage these colors, text, numbers, and other values.
content.paragraph3: For designers, the two may seem abstract but are actually inseparable in practice; for engineers, Design Tokens are like variables in code.
